opus-5.5.text:
So when I started my PhD at NYU, I came in with a fairly traditional linguistics background. I was interested in morphology and in how people process words, and the computational side was more of a tool for me. You'd build a probabilistic model, compute something like surprisal or entropy for each word or morpheme, and then see whether that predicted reading times or brain responses in an MEG experiment. The model was a measuring instrument, not really a theory of the mind in itself.

Over the course of the PhD that view shifted. I started taking more seriously the idea that the models themselves could be hypotheses about what the mind is doing. Instead of just asking "does this quantity correlate with behavior," you could ask "what would a learner need to have built in to end up behaving like humans do, given the kind of data a child actually sees?" That's a very different question. It gets at learnability, at inductive biases, at debates about innateness that linguists had been having for decades, mostly without being able to test them directly.

And around the end of my PhD, neural networks were starting to work again for language. That was surprising to a lot of people in linguistics, including me. Many of us had absorbed the idea that these kinds of statistical learners couldn't possibly pick up hierarchical syntactic structure without strong built-in constraints. Suddenly there were systems you could actually train and probe. You could ask, for example, whether a network learns subject-verb agreement across intervening material, which requires something like sensitivity to structure rather than just linear proximity.

So I went from seeing computation as a way to quantify predictions for experiments to seeing it as a way to run something close to controlled experiments on learners themselves. I'm still cautious. These models aren't humans, and they get far more data than children do. But that combination, treating models as candidate learners and comparing them carefully against human behavior, became the core of how I think about the field.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift toward treating models as hypotheses and using them to study learners, but it does not say this approach was more promising than purely experimental approaches.

r002.rationale: It frames computation as a way to predict and study human behavior in experiments and to test candidate models of human learning, rather than as a project of building AI for its own sake.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I started my PhD, I was coming at things very much from a theoretical linguistics background, and I'll admit I was fairly skeptical of a lot of computational work. My sense at the time was that the models people were building, especially the statistical ones, were sort of engineering artifacts. They could predict the next word reasonably well, but it wasn't clear to me what they were telling us about how humans actually represent language in their heads.

What changed over the course of the PhD was partly just getting my hands dirty. I started working with probabilistic models of sentence processing, and I realized that the computational framing forced me to be much more explicit about my assumptions than the theoretical work had. If you want to claim that people are predicting upcoming words, you have to say what the prediction is based on, what the probability distribution looks like, how it interacts with memory. Writing that down as a model, and then testing it against reading times or eye-tracking data, was really clarifying. A lot of the things I thought were settled turned out to be surprisingly hard to pin down once you had to formalize them.

The other shift was in how I thought about the relationship between the model and the mind. I stopped thinking of the question as "is this model the right theory of human cognition" and started thinking of models as tools for asking sharper questions. A model that makes the wrong prediction is still useful, because it tells you precisely where your assumptions break down. That reframing made me much more comfortable with the idea that you could learn something from a system that's clearly not a human, as long as you're careful about what you're actually inferring from it.

And honestly, that mindset is what I carried into working with neural networks later on. I don't treat them as theories of the mind in any straightforward sense, but I do think they're incredibly useful for testing claims about what kinds of structure you can and can't acquire from particular kinds of experience. That's a question linguists have been arguing about for decades, and suddenly we had systems where you could actually run the experiment.

r001.rationale: The response describes computational models as useful for sharpening questions and testing claims, but does not say Linzen came to see them as more promising than purely experimental approaches.

r002.rationale: The response discusses models tested against human reading-time and eye-tracking data, and neural networks as tools for studying learnable structure. It does not clearly distinguish using machine learning to understand experimental human behavior from doing AI research per se.

astra-6.text:
During my PhD, I became more interested in using computational models to make theories about language precise. You can have a verbal explanation of how people understand a sentence, but once you try to implement it, you discover how many assumptions you haven’t specified.

I also came to appreciate the distinction between building a system that performs a task well and explaining how people perform that task. A model might make very good predictions without using the same mechanisms that humans use. So the question becomes: what evidence would let us distinguish those possibilities? You want to look at where the model succeeds, where it fails, and whether those patterns resemble human behavior. That made computational approaches seem especially useful to me as tools for testing hypotheses, rather than as explanations on their own.

r001.rationale: The response says computational models are useful for making theories precise and testing hypotheses, but it does not compare them with purely experimental approaches or say they became more promising.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes task performance from explaining human mechanisms, but does not state that Linzen used machine learning to understand behavior in experiments rather than pursuing AI research per se.

sol-6.1.text:
During my PhD, I became more interested in using computational models to make theories about language precise. A verbal theory can sound convincing, but implementing it forces you to spell out your assumptions and see whether they actually produce the behavior you’re trying to explain.

I also became more cautious about what success tells us. A model can do well on a task for reasons that are very different from the reasons humans do well. So the question becomes more specific: where does it behave like a person, where does it diverge, and what can those differences tell us about the mechanisms involved?

r001.rationale: The response says computational models help make language theories precise, but does not compare them with purely experimental approaches or say they became more promising.

r002.rationale: The response discusses comparing model behavior with human behavior, but does not distinguish using machine learning to understand human experiments from conducting AI research.
